content_html:
Static cling increases when synthetic fabrics, dry air, and friction combine, especially in the dryer. To reduce it, avoid overdrying, separate items that generate a lot of charge, and use anti-static options compatible with care labels. Adding more heat often makes the problem worse by removing even more moisture from fibers.

Stop drying when clothes are dry rather than much later

Running long after a load is dry promotes static and fabric wear. Use a moisture sensor if it works correctly or shorten timed drying for light loads; still make sure thicker items have actually dried.

Separate synthetics from fibers that retain more moisture

Polyester and other synthetics can build substantial charge as they rub together. Drying part of the load separately or removing synthetics earlier can reduce the effect while still following care labels.

Use anti-static products only when compatible

Dryer sheets or fabric softeners can reduce static, but they leave coatings that are not suitable for every garment. Activewear, towels, and technical fabrics can lose performance; check labels before using a product by habit.

Very low indoor humidity can contribute

In winter, extremely dry indoor air promotes charge buildup. Keep household humidity in a comfortable range that is also safe for the building; do not dampen stored clothes or raise humidity until condensation forms on windows or walls.
